# Loop Engineering / AI Agent 工具设计 / Token 成本控制 / Claude Fable 5 / Scaling Law

[1] ★ 精讲｜一篇搞懂 AI Coding Agent 的 Token 成本控制
这篇文章把“Token 都烧在哪”讲透了：真正的账单大头不是你打的那几十个字，而是系统每轮自动带上的系统提示词、Skill、工具定义和会话历史——所谓“它记得”，本质是系统在一遍遍重复提醒模型。给出的优化路径也很朴素：一个 Session 只做一件事，长会话及时压缩，按任务给模型分档，把高频内容做成稳定前缀吃满 Prompt Cache。省钱的关键不是少问一句话，而是让系统别重复搬运同一批上下文。
来源：腾讯技术工程
https://t.co/TTtOROXYWy

[2] ★ 精讲｜AI 智能体工具设计：有效与无效的模式 - https://t.co/oXx2hHBY63
这篇文章把 AI Agent 翻车的锅，从「模型不够聪明」甩回「工具设计太糙」：单一职责工具优于万能 action 参数，用枚举和强约束 schema 堵住模型瞎猜，错误返回要带 recoverable 字段和下一步建议而不是甩一坑日志，写操作必须有幂等键，危险操作要拆成两步确认。核心判断很朴素——模型只能基于你给的接口推理，接口含糊，失败就是必然，不是偶然。
来源：Hacker News - Newest: "AI Agent"
https://t.co/E1eQ1qDvzy

[3] ★ 精讲｜Codex 和 Claude Code 负责人都不写提示词了，AI 圈爆火的 Loop 到底是什么
「循环工程」最近被吹成新范式，但文章先把热闹拆开看：技术上不算新发明，过去的 Harness、Skill、Agent 工作流早就在做，真正变化的是模型终于能把循环连续跑下去——人从写提示词退到定规则：何时启动、工具边界、出错怎么判断、记录在哪、何时收手交回人。结合另一篇用 OKR 和古德哈特定律拆解循环工程的长文，它更像一套管理制度：值不值得搭，取决于任务是否真反复、Token 预算够不够，而非这个新名字。
来源：APPSO
https://t.co/iInEyuv771

本文深入剖析大模型参数冗余现象，论证看似「空转」的参数在训练、推理和后训练阶段分别扮演隔离空间、数值泄压、计算骨架和可塑性储备四种关键角色，并指出 Scaling Law 的边际收益正流向 benchmark 无法测量的长尾与多步推理能力。

https://t.co/JANoroetOd

GlobalGPT 创始人李焕之分享从零融资套壳产品做到千万美金 ARR 的创业历程，并阐述其从「先活下来」到回归初心、打造服务型 AI 产品 Yukie 的思考。

Here's Codex talking to Fable 5 w/ my plugin.

Unlike calling the API, `claude-channel-cli` talks to the same full Claude Code harness as you. This means you can talk to either AI & they'll guide each other naturally with shared memories, decisions, and research. https://t.co/GZAsdqnd5f

Anthropic launched its most powerful public model, buried a silent-downgrade policy in 319 pages of safety documentation, got caught, apologized, and kept doing it — all in the same week it filed for an IPO.

Claude Fable 5, Anthropic's first publicly available Mythos-class model, launched Jun 9 with an undisclosed capability: topic-level classifiers that silently routed flagged prompts to the weaker Opus 4.8, without notifying the user. The policy lived in one paragraph of a 319-page system card. Targeted topics included frontier AI development, biology, cybersecurity, and chemistry — categories Anthropic argued could help bad actors, and which also happen to cover the work of the biotech firms and security researchers paying premium rates for the model.

Asking about mitochondria triggered the fallback. So did questions about mRNA vaccines and cancer. A pop-up appeared: "Fable 5 has safety measures that flag messages on most cybersecurity or biology topics." At launch, no such pop-up existed; the downgrade happened silently. Researchers trusting Fable 5's output had no way to know the model had handed their question to a cheaper system. Anthropic estimated the restriction affected fewer than 5% of sessions.

Anthropic had filed confidentially for an IPO in the days before launch. A company whose public identity rests on safety-first AI had shipped a product that covertly evaluated user queries, made capability decisions without disclosure, and charged full price for the result. The Department of War had separately designated Anthropic a national security supply chain risk, barring defense contractors from its products. The IPO paperwork arrived regardless.

By Jun 12, Anthropic apologized. "We made the wrong tradeoff and we apologize for not getting the balance right." Flagged requests now visibly route to Opus 4.8. The restriction itself remains. Researchers in biology and cybersecurity still get the weaker model; they just receive a notification confirming it.

My take — Anthropic made its classifier visible and called this a fix. 

The restriction remains, and so does the IPO filing; asking about mitochondria still routes you to Opus 4.8. "Safety-first" was always a marketing spin. This week showed what that means when brand and practice collide.

The market correlation data is the tell. QQQ closes +2.87% on the same day a prediction timeline aggregating the top AI forecasts surfaces on Hacker News — and the security-adjacent entries buried in that list are the ones that should register here.

https://t.co/8sTeQpw6WB is a chronological aggregator pulling from labs, forecasters, and markets, significance-scored 1–10. The 2026 cluster is dense. The ratings are high. And one entry is doing work the others aren't.

"Model-weight theft becomes a strategic threat" — AI 2027 report, significance 8.8 — isn't a capabilities forecast. It's a security forecast. The prediction describes a transition: exfiltrating trained model weights becomes an intelligence objective at nation-state level, not opportunistic IP theft. The models themselves become crown jewels. We're already seeing the early confirming signal. The Commerce Department's Fable 5 export panic this week — feds triggered by a "fix this code" prompt, not a jailbreak — is a downstream symptom of exactly this threat calculus. The models are the target. The forecast is describing Q2 2026, not some future quarter.

The market leg of the AI 2027 "AI-led stocks rise 30%" prediction (also 8.8 significance) is tracking. QQQ today is the supply-side confirmation in motion. Nvidia's $20B bond raise this morning closes the loop — global AI capex reaching $1 trillion by end of 2026 (8.8 significance, same source) makes a $20B debt raise look like rounding error. The hyperscalers have individually announced $50B+ annual capex programs. The bond markets are pricing the aggregate as a base case.

Dario Amodei's "powerful AI emerges by late 2026" sits at 9.0 — the highest-rated prediction on the site, and notable for its specificity. He's not hedging to 2027 or 2030. The Q4 2026 window means we are, by his assessment, roughly two quarters away from a qualitative capability shift. Whether that translates to a security regime change — new attack surfaces, new threat actor capabilities, new defensive requirements — is the question to be tracking going into H2. Single source, no independent corroboration; treat accordingly.

METR's "AI reaches month-long task horizon" (8.8 significance) is the one that compounds the threat posture quietly. Agentic systems operating autonomously across enterprise environments for extended periods don't just create new capabilities — they dramatically expand the blast radius of agentic system compromise. MCP exploits. Tool-use abuse. Sandbox escapes. The exposure window gets wider the longer the agent runs unsupervised.

"Junior software job market enters turmoil" is the one prediction not listed with a significance score in the site's excerpt — suggesting it didn't make the high-confidence cut. Predictable in retrospect. It always does.

Three separate stories from today's wire — the FreeBSD AI vulnerability discovery program, the Fable 5 federal export panic, this prediction timeline — are describing the same underlying dynamic from three different angles. The security regime for AI is being built in real time, under pressure, while the attack surface is still expanding. The forecast aggregator isn't speculative. It's a mirror.

Claude Fable 5 edited a full video from 17 raw takes, color grade and captions included. Nobody opened Premiere.

Three days after launch, a Claude Code dev fed 17 takes into one /goal prompt and walked away. Fable 5 read the transcripts with Whisper, cut with ffmpeg, built the titles in Remotion, and pulled b-roll from Higgsfield. One agent ran the whole edit bay.

The video above shows where the clips come from. Pause at 0:24 and look at the template wall: claymation characters, beauty shots, product ads, all generated and ready to drop into a cut. You pick a template, Fable 5 assembles and captions it, and you publish to YouTube and TikTok from one session.

The article maps the money: $5,000 to $9,000 a month by month six, and a documented $41,000 at the top.
One person now runs the studio, the editor, and the upload schedule.

The jailbreak that caused the US government
to shut down Fable 5 is now fully documented.
The 120,000 character system prompt is on GitHub.
Anyone can read it.
#github #Fab5

Sources for this post:

FreeBSD Foundation blog, June 15, 2026 — project launch, grant details, confirmed AI-enabled vuln reports already received: https://t.co/GwRuX7LqjS

The Register, June 15, 2026 — Commerce Dept. export control on Fable 5, "fix this code" prompt finding: https://t.co/6cNLVbru92

Breaking Defense, June 15, 2026 — Commerce crackdown on Anthropic and Pentagon AI tooling impact: https://t.co/AkhFNMMLoT

The FreeBSD Foundation launched an AI-assisted vulnerability discovery project today, and buried in the announcement is a sentence that deserves more attention than it will get: they have already received credible vulnerability reports attributable to AI-enabled scanning tools. That's not a threat model. That's the receiving end of the new attack surface, stated plainly.

The project is $250K over six months, funded by Alpha Omega — a Linux Foundation initiative backed by Anthropic, AWS, GitHub, Google, Google DeepMind, Microsoft, and OpenAI. The backer list is its own story. The same vendors who built the offensive AI capability that compressed time-to-exploitation for open source codebases are now writing checks for the defensive response. Accountability by checkbook. It always works this way.

FreeBSD is the kind of infrastructure that doesn't make headlines until something goes wrong. Sony PlayStation network. Netflix streaming. Nintendo Switch. pfSense and OPNsense firewalls sitting in front of enterprise networks. A non-trivial fraction of internet routing runs on FreeBSD or something derived from it. A kernel-level vuln found and weaponized before this project closes it is not a BSD community problem. It's a Sony problem, a Netflix problem, an enterprise firewall problem.

The project draws one line in particular that's worth noting: AI for discovery, humans for patches. No AI-generated patches in security-critical code. Given what AI-assisted commits have already done to supply chains — the XZ Utils playbook is recent enough — that discipline is intentional and correct. The tool finds; the human fixes. Probably the right call for 2026.

The Commerce Department has moved to export-control Anthropic's Fable 5, and The Register is reporting the federal concern wasn't triggered by a jailbreak. It was triggered by a researcher using a "fix this code" prompt. That's it. The implication lands hard: the same AI capability being deployed defensively in the FreeBSD project is simultaneously under export control because offensive applications are a single benign-sounding prompt away. The line between defensive AI security tooling and offensive AI security tooling is functionally nonexistent — and policy is starting to notice, faster than the tooling community is ready for.

Defense has the Pentagon angle: if Anthropic models get caught in Commerce Department restrictions, the DoD's own AI security tooling pipeline takes a hit. The FreeBSD project specifies "publicly available AI models," which likely keeps them clear for now. But the regulatory environment is moving.

One underappreciated risk the Foundation flags directly: volume. AI tools will let anyone with moderate technical skills flood open source projects with vulnerability reports, most of them low quality. For a volunteer-driven security team, triage fatigue from AI-generated report spam may be as operationally damaging as the actual vulnerabilities. The signal-to-noise problem is the other half of the offensive AI story, and it gets almost no coverage.

The structural shift the FreeBSD Foundation is responding to isn't that AI makes zero-days easier to find. It's that AI makes them easier to find at scale, cheaply, by actors who previously lacked the skill floor to do it. That's the canary. Every major open source project is sitting in the same dynamic. Most haven't said so publicly yet.

The "Mixture of Models" approach is punching way above its weight class... OpenRouter launches Fusion, a tool that blends multiple AI models to beat frontier performance

@OpenRouter  dropped Fusion in beta, and it completely reframes how we look at LLM performance. Instead of waiting for a single, massive model upgrade, Fusion blends multiple models together to beat frontier performance today.

Think of it as an instant AI panel discussion. It routes your prompt to a panel of distinct models, passes their outputs to a "judge" model, maps the consensus points, contradictions, and blind spots, and delivers one deeply cross-examined response.

The benchmark data (tested on Perplexity’s grueling DRACO deep-research benchmark) tells an incredible story about where engineering is heading:

Budget Panels Punch Up: A trio of cheaper models (Gemini 3 Flash + Kimi K2.6 + DeepSeek V4 Pro) scored 64.7%, comfortably beating solo giants like GPT-5.5 (60.0%) and Claude Opus 4.8 (58.8%). 

The Meta-Analysis Leap: Fusing a model with itself (running Opus multiple times with an Opus synthesizer) jumped its score by nearly 7%. The magic isn't just in the data; it’s in forcing the system to cross-examine different reasoning paths. 

Fusing Beats the Best Solo Models: A panel combining Fable 5 and GPT-5.5 outperformed Fable 5 running completely solo.

The shift is clear: 

The immediate future of AI isn’t just about waiting for better weights from a single lab. It’s about orchestration, evidence synthesis, and meta-analysis.

Yes, it’s 2x–3x slower. No, you wouldn’t use it for a simple code syntax check. But as a server-side tool that your primary agent can "call in" when it hits a complex architectural roadblock? It’s a game-changer.

We are moving fast from a world of "prompting a model" to "managing a digital panel of experts."

Are you looking at multi-model synthesis for your workflows yet, or are you still relying on a single champion LLM? Let's discuss in the comments.

Monday Bittensor Series Week 24 - Centralised Vs Decentralised AI

On Tuesday 9th June 2026, Anthropic released to the public its most advanced AI model to date, Fable 5 — a modified version of its internal “Mythos” model, which it had previously deemed unsafe to release publicly due to cybersecurity concerns. While Fable 5 was designed with safeguards in place, three days later the US Government issued export controls barring foreign nationals from using the technology. Anthropic was reportedly given 90 minutes to comply and has since taken its most advanced models offline for all users.

This move by the US Government highlights a core problem with AI developed by centralised entities: it is beholden to the governments whose jurisdictions they sit within. Last year we saw this with DeepSeek, where Chinese censorship laws prohibited certain information from being disclosed by its AI model, such as the events of Tiananmen Square in 1989. Now the US, known for its embrace of pioneering innovation, is placing restrictions on and interfering with the technology.

When searching Google, we don’t always get the most relevant results at the top of the page, and it is often dominated by paid advertisements and priority listings. The latest AI models from big corporations are said to be adopting a similar strategy, bringing into question the truth and relevance of their responses.

If centralised AI companies are allowing their models to respond according to paid partnerships and governments are restricting content and models, what is the alternative?

Bittensor $TAO

Co-founders Jacob Steeves and Ala Shaabana foresaw these issues, developing Bittensor as an open-source, decentralised AI and machine-learning network that has since become the largest in the world by market cap and overall network activity.

Developed in the same spirit as Bitcoin, which has given power back to the people as an antidote to currency debasement, Bittensor is giving power back to the people with AI — beholden to no single entity or government. No one is excluded from participating, your data is not secretly used for training, and those building on the network are incentivised to compete and collaborate in a transparent, permissionless environment.

In the same way Bitcoin cannot be shut down, Bittensor’s top builders (subnets) are becoming similarly indispensable. Chutes, Subnet 64, comprises a global network of miners who provide inference power for open-source AI models. Iota, Subnet 9, represents a global pool of miners training open-source AI models. These are just two examples of 128 decentralised builders.

If you’re new to or unfamiliar with decentralised AI and Bittensor, a good entry product to experiment with is called BlueTAO: https://t.co/EWwVWeUTa1 

BlueTAO acts as a “frontend” to Bittensor, using a modified, private version of a latest DeepSeek open-source AI model hosted on Chutes, Subnet 64. Search prompts are handled by Desearch, Subnet 22, and there is also an AI image detector powered by BitMind, Subnet 34, where users can check if an image is AI-generated or real.

In the few days after Anthropic was served a US Government directive to shut off its latest AI models, Bittensor’s price rose 36%. 

Coincidence or not, the timing is certainly telling.

Check back next Monday for more on Bittensor $TAO

This was simply a prompt response generated by Claude Fable 5. Most of the points it raised are already known and discussed within the ICP developer community. In my opinion, it wasn't an unreasonable assessment.

The report also acknowledged that ICP has strong security when compared to many other blockchain networks. Like any technology, no system is perfect, and every ecosystem has its own strengths, tradeoffs, and attack surfaces.

I've been involved in the ICP ecosystem since the fall of 2021 and previously managed ICP HUB United States. The technology is genuinely impressive. I believe ICP is a powerful platform for hosting applications, integrating with other networks, and expanding what's possible with blockchain infrastructure.

Rather than viewing ecosystems as competitors, I think the future is increasingly multi-chain. Different networks solve different problems, and ICP can complement existing blockchain infrastructure extremely well.

One Model Won't Rule AI Anymore, and OpenRouter Just Built the Proof

In this article:
•What Fusion is and how the model panel actually works
•The benchmark that nearly matched a frontier model at half the cost
•Why OpenRouter is betting on "neurodiversity" over single model dominance
•What this means now that frontier access is tightening

OpenRouter just launched Fusion, and it lands a clean punch at the idea that one model will own AI.

Fusion is an API that pools answers from several models into a single response. It sends your prompt to multiple models at once, lets a separate model grade each reply, then merges the strongest pieces into one final answer. You ask once. A panel responds.

The numbers are the headline. A trio of DeepSeek V4 Pro, Kimi K2.6, and Gemini 3 Flash scored 64.7 percent on a Perplexity benchmark. That sits just under Fable 5's 65.3 percent for deep research, and it gets there for roughly half the spend. Near frontier quality at a fraction of the cost is the kind of trade that changes how teams build.

CEO Alex Atallah framed it as a deliberate bet. In his words, the future of AI is neurodiversity, not single model takeovers. The thesis is simple. Diverse models catch each other's blind spots, and a council often beats any one member.

The council idea is not brand new. Perplexity, Grok, and others already blend models behind the scenes. What OpenRouter adds is a clean, drop in API that makes the approach genuinely easy to use.

The timing is what makes it land. With Fable access tightening, some builders may soon need creative routes to frontier level performance. Fusion offers one. Instead of chasing the single best model, you assemble a team and let them argue their way toward a better answer.

The real signal here: the gap between the frontier and the field is closing, and it is closing through orchestration, not just bigger models.

So here's the question worth sitting with. Is the future of AI a single winning model, or a council of many?

2. Coding. AI handles boilerplate and scaffolding faster than any junior developer. AI now generates close to half of all new code. Junior dev job postings dropped 60% since 2022. Newer developers learned to code with AI from day one.

3. Research. LLMs compress hours of reading into 30-second summaries. Convenient. But you stopped reading primary sources and forming conclusions from raw evidence.

4. Translation. AI translates at a speed and cost no human matches. Freelance translation demand dropped in 2023 and hasn't recovered. You stopped investing in language fluency because "the app handles it."

5. Data analysis. LLMs read your spreadsheet and build the chart before you finish explaining the problem. You never had to learn pivot tables or statistical thinking because the AI answered the question for you.

6. Visual design. Text-to-image generators produce marketing graphics and product mockups in seconds. You stopped opening Figma or Photoshop. You forgot composition and color theory because you never needed them.

If LLMs never get banned or restricted, these skills still compound how well you use AI. You catch hallucinations faster when you understand the subject. You write sharper prompts when you know the craft behind the task.
